title: Ceva's Theorem: Non-Euclidean Extensions via Unified Ratio Framework
description: Extends Ceva's theorem to spherical and hyperbolic geometry using an abstract generalized framework. All three versions — trigonometric (Euclidean), spherical, and hyperbolic — reduce to the same algebraic identity: a product of three ratios ρ(a)/ρ(b) equals 1, where ρ is the identity (Euclidean), sin (spherical), or sinh (hyperbolic). The formalization includes flat-limit theorems proving that both sin(x)/x → 1 and sinh(x)/x → 1 as x → 0, formally connecting the non-Euclidean versions to the Euclidean case for small triangles.

overview.historicalContext: Giovanni Ceva's theorem (De lineis rectis, 1678) characterizes concurrent cevians in Euclidean triangles. Non-Euclidean versions were developed in the 19th century following the discovery of hyperbolic geometry by Bolyai and Lobachevsky. The spherical version was known earlier in the context of spherical trigonometry, used in geodesy and astronomy. Athanase Papadopoulos and others have studied hyperbolic analogues of classical theorems. The key observation — that replacing linear distances by sin (spherical) or sinh (hyperbolic) preserves the product-equals-one concurrency condition — reflects the general principle that non-Euclidean geometry is governed by the same algebraic identities with trigonometric substitutions.
overview.problemStatement: Do analogues of Ceva's theorem hold in spherical and hyperbolic geometry? The answer is yes: in spherical geometry, cevians of a geodesic triangle are concurrent iff sin(BD)·sin(CE)·sin(AF) = sin(DC)·sin(EA)·sin(FB) for arc-length segments; in hyperbolic geometry, the condition is sinh(BD)·sinh(CE)·sinh(AF) = sinh(DC)·sinh(EA)·sinh(FB) for hyperbolic distances. Both reduce to the same algebraic identity as the Euclidean case.
overview.proofStrategy: The algebraic core of Ceva's theorem is: given six positive reals a, b, c, d, e, f, the product (a/b)(c/d)(e/f) = 1 iff ace = bdf. This is purely division algebra and requires only positivity of the denominators. For each geometry, the relevant quantities (sin of arc lengths for spherical, sinh of hyperbolic distances) are positive in the appropriate domain. The positivity of sin on (0,π) is from Mathlib; the positivity of sinh on (0,∞) is proved from the strict monotonicity of exp. The flat limits are derived from HasDerivAt at zero.
keyInsights: All three Ceva conditions are instances of a single algebraic identity: ρ(a)/ρ(b) · ρ(c)/ρ(d) · ρ(e)/ρ(f) = 1 ↔ ρ(a)ρ(c)ρ(e) = ρ(b)ρ(d)ρ(f)
sinh_pos_of_pos follows from exp being strictly monotone: exp(x) > 1 and exp(-x) < 1 for x > 0
The derivative HasDerivAt.tendsto_slope_zero converts the derivative of sin (resp. sinh) at 0 to the limit of the difference quotient
The flat limit theorems provide the formal connection: as triangles shrink, all three Ceva conditions converge to the same Euclidean form
The structure GeneralizedCevianConfig separates the configuration from the geometry, enabling reuse of the algebraic proof

conclusion.summary: The non-Euclidean extensions of Ceva's theorem are formally verified with 18 theorems and 0 sorries. The abstract framework (GeneralizedCevianConfig, ceva_unified_principle) cleanly separates the geometry from the algebra, making the proof structure transparent. The flat-limit theorems provide a rigorous formal connection between the three geometric settings.
conclusion.implications: The unified approach suggests a general pattern for non-Euclidean geometry: classical theorems involving ratios of lengths often have non-Euclidean versions obtained by replacing lengths with sin (spherical) or sinh (hyperbolic). This pattern appears in the law of sines, Menelaus' theorem, and trigonometric identities. The sinh derivative proof (hasDerivAt_sinh) is a useful standalone result not easily found in Mathlib.
openQuestions: Can the unified Ceva framework be extended to arbitrary curvature κ using the functions sin_κ (Jacobi sine for curvature κ)?
What is the hyperbolic analogue of Menelaus' theorem in this framework?
Can the abstract GeneralizedCevianConfig be used to prove non-Euclidean versions of other concurrence theorems (e.g., hyperbolic angle bisectors)?
Does the flat limit argument extend to a formal proof that the hyperbolic and spherical Ceva conditions converge to the Euclidean one for triangles on a manifold of shrinking curvature?
